hints.title: Find the boundaries
hints.body: A product changes sign only at a factor zero. Mark −4, −3 and 1 for the cubic, and −2 and 2 for the quadratic.
hints.recap: Solve each product inequality by testing the intervals between its zeros.
hints.pitfall: The factor written as one minus x has the opposite sign from x minus one.
hints.pause: Find where the simpler quadratic product is negative.

recall.reminder: Solve each product inequality by testing the intervals between its zeros.

hints.title: Intersect the sign restrictions
hints.body: First solve the quadratic inequality. On the interval you obtain, determine the signs of each factor in the cubic product.
hints.recap: For simultaneous inequalities, retain only inputs that satisfy both conditions.
hints.pitfall: Strict inequalities exclude points where either product is zero.
hints.pause: Complete the factor-sign check inside the quadratic interval and write the overlap.

recall.reminder: For simultaneous inequalities, retain only inputs that satisfy both conditions.

solution:
The quadratic (x+2)(x−2) is negative exactly when −2<x<2. On this interval both x+4 and x+3 are positive. Consequently (x+4)(x+3)(1−x)>0 is equivalent to 1−x>0, or x<1.

Combining these restrictions gives −2<x<1, option B. At x=−2 the quadratic product is zero, and at x=1 the cubic product is zero, so neither endpoint is included.

As a full sign-chart check, the cubic is positive on x<−4 and −3<x<1. Intersecting that union with (−2,2) gives the same answer.
knowledgePattern: Intersect cubic and quadratic sign regions
